newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Turkish Cypriot leader Denktash is tough veteran.
newsitem.headline: Turkish Cypriot leader Denktash is tough veteran.

text.p: Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash has spent more than three decades at the forefront of the political fight for his community on the divided island of Cyprus, maintaining the same firm stance over the years.

"I take an oath that the Turkish Cypriot community will never become a minority, nor will the island ever become Greek," he said in 1963, three years after independence from Britain and two months before intercommunal fighting broke out.
In November 1996, he was still on the same track.

"The Turks in Cyprus will never accept being brought down to the status of a minority and neither Turkey nor the Turkish Cypriots will let this island become a Greek island," he said at a ceremony to mark the 13th anniversary of the self-declared Turkish Cypriot state he dominates.

The 73-year-old, undaunted by a heart attack in March 1996, can be expected to stick to that line when he meets his longtime rival, Greek Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides, for U.N.-sponsored talks between July 9 to 13.

The two are due to meet outside New York in another tentative bid to end the division of Cyprus, split since Turkey invaded in 1974 in response to a Greek Cypriot coup backed by the military government then ruling in Athens.
Denktash's position is now complicated by European Union attempts to bring his Greek Cypriot adversaries towards full membership of the union.
Turkish Cypriots fear even further isolation if EU accession talks with the internationally recognised Greek Cypriot government, due to start in 1998, are successful.

The Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, created with Denktash as president in 1983 and recognised only by Ankara, could face the difficult choice of integrating with Turkey -- thus dividing the island more permanently -- or making concessions to the Greek Cypriots, by then backed by Europe.

Denktash, with a record as a tough negotiator, is seen as the only man who can sell a peace deal to his community. Rotund and affable, he has demonstrated an incisive wit and considerable diplomatic skills throughout his career.
"I would not underestimate the difficulties of confronting him," a U.N. official said.
Denktash's performances in past U.N.-sponsored talks on reunification have won him three presidential election campaigns.
All attempts to reunify the island in a federation have failed.

Turkish Cypriots insist on separate zones in any federation and strictly regulated rights of settlement and property. Denktash fears the 160,000 Turkish Cypriots could be dominated by the 600,000 Greek Cypriots in a unified state.

He saw off a serious challenge to his leadership by former protege Dervis Eroglu, who jeered at him as "the sultan", in 1993. The struggle ended with Denktash's son Serdar becoming more powerful. Denktash junior is now a contender to succeed him.
But Denktash's success at home has not been matched abroad. Only Turkey recognises the Turkish Cypriot state, which is under limited EU trade sanctions. Ankara maintains 30,000 troops there.
In the 1960s, as now, Denktash's opposite negotiating partner was Clerides, president of the Greek Cypriot south.
Denktash, the son of a judge, was born on January 27, 1924, in the southwestern coastal town of Paphos. He went to school on the island and won a scholarship to study law in London.

He was at Lincoln's Inn from 1944 to 1947. He later returned to Cyprus and plunged straight into politics as a member of the Consultative Assembly set up by the British colonial administration. He was solicitor general in 1956 and 1957.

Denktash helped to establish the TMT, a Turkish Cypriot paramilitary group. It was set up to oppose the Greek Cypriot EOKA, which waged guerrilla warfare against the British in the 1950s with the aim of "enosis", uniting the island with Greece.
Turkish Cypriots began to react against demands for enosis by proposing "taksim" (partition) as an alternative.
In the late 1950s Denktash was elected chairman of the Federation of Turkish-Cypriot Associations, becoming the number two man in the community after the late Fadil Kucuk.

Cyprus gained independence in 1960 under a constitution designed to share power between the communities, but tensions erupted into fighting in 1963. The next year Denktash returned from a U.N. Security Council meeting to find himself banned from Cyprus.
When he tried to smuggle himself back in 1967, he was captured, detained and sent to Turkey.
He returned a year later as Turkish Cypriot negotiator and spent six years in hard, fruitless bargaining with Clerides, then president of the House of Representatives.
Denktash, a keen amateur photographer and dog owner, is married and has twin daughters, a son and grandchildren.
Two other children, a boy and a girl, died young, while his eldest son was killed in a car crash in December 1985.
